cards.title: The 1/3–2/3 conjecture
cards.formal: For every integer n≥2 and every partial order P=([n],≤_P) that is not a total order, do there exist incomparable elements x,y∈[n] such that e(P)/3≤e_P(x,y)≤2e(P)/3?
cards.why: Asks for the sharp universal quality of a comparison when sorting with partial information. It connects uncertainty among compatible rankings to an extremal property of every finite partial order.

cards.definitions: [n]={1,…,n}. A partial order ≤_P is a reflexive, antisymmetric and transitive relation. Distinct x,y are incomparable when neither x≤_P y nor y≤_P x; P is a total order when no such pair exists. A linear extension is a bijection L:[n]→[n] with L(a)<L(b) whenever a≤_P b and a≠b. Let E(P) be the finite nonempty set of all linear extensions, e(P)=|E(P)|, and e_P(x,y)=|{L∈E(P):L(x)<L(y)}|. Equivalently choose L uniformly from E(P), so the displayed interval requires Pr[L(x)<L(y)]∈[1/3,2/3], including endpoints. The pair x,y may depend on the entire poset. This is an existence proposition over all finite orders, with no width, height or representation restriction and no algorithmic requirement. Width is the largest size of a set of pairwise incomparable elements; height is the largest size of a totally ordered subset. For context, the balance constant is β(P)=max_{x≠y} min{e_P(x,y),e_P(y,x)}/e(P); this card uses β to avoid conflicting δ conventions across sources.

context_blocks.text: A partial order records comparisons already known, and its linear extensions are all complete rankings still compatible with that information. The conjecture says that unless only one ranking remains, some unresolved comparison splits these possible rankings into two substantial groups. Neither outcome may leave more than two thirds of them. The distribution is uniform over whole rankings, not over the currently available choices in a stepwise topological sort.

Take three elements with a<b and c unrelated to both. The three linear extensions are abc, acb and cab. The probability that a precedes c is 2/3, while the probability that b precedes c is 1/3. No incomparable pair is closer to a half. This small example shows that the universal interval cannot be narrowed to [1/3+η,2/3−η] for any η>0. In a total order every pair instead has probability zero or one, which explains the excluded case.

Uniform local choices need not produce uniform extensions. In the same example, choosing randomly between the two initially minimal elements a and c gives cab probability 1/2, and gives abc and acb probability 1/4 each. Those are different from the required probabilities 1/3 each. Fixing the probability space prevents a superficially similar random-ordering question from replacing the conjecture.

Brightwell, Felsner and Trotter prove the weaker universal bound β(P)≥(5−√5)/10≈0.2764. It already guarantees an informative comparison and improves the earlier 3/11 bound of Kahn and Saks. The requested value 1/3 is a sharper extremal constant, rather than the first guarantee of any fixed positive balance.

The conjecture is known for substantial classes, including width-two and height-two orders, and orders whose cover graph is a forest. Width limits how many elements can be mutually incomparable; height limits the length of a chain. These are distinct restrictions, and neither covers arbitrary finite orders. The Chan–Pak survey states the general question separately from this collection of positive cases.

Aires and Kahn obtain stronger asymptotic balance under size hypotheses: for example β(P) tends to 1/2 when width is at least a fixed positive fraction of the number of elements. Their 2025 paper still states the unrestricted 1/3–2/3 bound as a conjecture. A result for a sequence of sufficiently wide orders leaves narrower and exceptional finite orders uncovered.

Gupta’s July 2026 revision reports an exhaustive verification of the stronger Gold Partition property through fourteen elements, implying the balance conjecture for those sizes. Its arithmetic and archived artifacts are described in the paper; this review did not rerun the census. A verified finite range, however large its enumeration, does not establish the universal statement.

cards.answer_criterion: Prove the displayed inequalities for at least one incomparable pair in every finite non-total order, or exhibit a finite non-total order for which every incomparable pair has probability outside [1/3,2/3]. All probabilities refer to the uniform distribution on its full set of linear extensions.

sentences: A partial order records known comparisons, and its linear extensions are all compatible complete rankings.
The conjecture asks whether every finite non-total order has an incomparable pair that appears in either relative order in at least one third of all extensions.
The extensions are weighted uniformly, and both endpoints of the interval are allowed.
A three-element order with only one comparison shows that the constant one third cannot be improved universally.
A resolution would identify the sharp balance guarantee for a comparison in sorting with partial information.

cards.title: Determine the pancake numbers
cards.formal: Determine f(n), the maximum over permutations of n symbols of the minimum number of prefix reversals needed to put the permutation in sorted order, for arbitrary n.
cards.why: A canonical extremal question about sorting with a highly restricted operation, equivalently the diameter of a natural permutation graph. Matching exact bounds would identify worst-case rearrangement cost beyond the known separated linear estimates.

importance.reason: A canonical extremal problem about the power of restricted sorting operations.

category_assignment.reason: The requested output is the exact extremal prefix-reversal distance over all permutations, rather than an efficient sorting implementation. It spans permutation combinatorics and restricted operations without requiring an algorithmic target.

cards.definitions: For n≥1, S_n is the set of permutations π=(π₁,…,π_n) of [n]={1,…,n}. For 2≤j≤n, a prefix reversal r_j sends π to (π_j,π_{j−1},…,π₁,π_{j+1},…,π_n). Each reversal costs one, regardless of j. Let d_n(π) be the least length of a finite reversal sequence sending π to (1,…,n), with the empty sequence allowed. Define f(n)=max_{π∈S_n}d_n(π); thus f(1)=0. Reversals generate S_n, so all these minima and maxima are finite. Equivalently f(n) is the diameter of the undirected Cayley graph on S_n with these prefix reversals. This is the unsigned, or unburnt, problem: no signs or orientations are tracked. Suffix reversals, arbitrary interval reversals and repeated symbols are not permitted. The remaining ambiguity concerns what general description of f is required as an answer, not the definition of f itself.

context_blocks.text: A stack is represented from top to bottom by a permutation of pancake sizes. The spatula can turn over an initial segment, so one move changes the order of several entries but always includes the top. The pancake number is the worst possible optimal flip count at a given stack size. It measures the power of this restricted operation, rather than the number of comparisons used by ordinary sorting.

For three pancakes, 132 can be sorted in three flips: 132→312→213→123, with prefix lengths 2,3,2. It cannot be sorted in two: its one-step neighbors are 312 and 231, whereas the sorted stack’s one-step neighbors are 213 and 321. These sets are disjoint. The six states can all be sorted within three moves, so f(3)=3. A flip count for one stack and a worst-case upper bound play different roles in such an equality.

Chitturi and coauthors give f(n)≤(18/11)n+O(1). Both the known lower and upper bounds are linear, but their leading coefficients remain separated. Merely proving f(n)=Θ(n) would restate an already known order of growth.

Peczarski’s 2026 note extends the lower bound to f(n)≥floor((15n+9)/14) for n≥6, improving coverage of stack sizes. The statement is given in the preprint and the author’s February exposition. It does not match the universal upper-bound coefficient.
Cibulka computed exact values through n=19, where f(19)=22. A finite table gives rigorous information about those sizes without determining the sequence at arbitrary n.

Amano’s near-(15/14)n sorting bound applies to a particular family used in lower-bound constructions, not every permutation. An upper bound on that family cannot be substituted for a universal upper bound on f.
Bulteau, Fertin and Rusu establish NP-hardness of finding the optimum for a supplied stack. That input-specific computational problem differs from describing the maximum optimum as a function of n.

Jäger and Oijid’s January 2026 result concerns the signed starting stack (−1,…,−n) and settles its optimum for an additional parity class. This is a different extremal question from the unburnt diameter defined here.

The benchmark target still needs specification. For each fixed n, the finite graph definition already permits exact computation without a runtime limit. The imported request to “determine f(n)” does not specify what must improve on that existing computation. This card records the mathematical quantity and known bounds while leaving that acceptance requirement unresolved; it does not silently replace exact determination with an asymptotic or efficient-algorithm question.

cards.answer_criterion: The source requests exact determination of f(n) for every n, which would require a matching universal upper bound and a stack attaining that value at each n. The acceptable general answer representation or computational guarantee remains unspecified; the existing finite graph search must not be mistaken for a new resolution.

meta.status_scope: No claim of exhaustive open-status verification
methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. We aim for benchmarks of 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. All three use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The possible 1,000-problem expansion has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The targets are 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. Top 100, Top 500 and the possible Top 1000 use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.

benchmark_selection.basis: Individual editorial review of saved titles, importance rationales, problem statements, source notes and working summaries. This is a review of importance and topical diversity, not a fresh verification of open status or completion of draft formulations. Importance scores are preserved.
